(Today through Tuesday)...
Issued at 245 AM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

Mild weather continues today ahead of low pressure that will 
approach the region this afternoon. The low will track quickly 
across the Ohio Valley late today into this evening with showers and 
a few thunderstorms accompanying an associated cold front. In its 
wake...a much cooler airmass will overspread the Ohio Valley as a 
strengthening upper level trough expands across the eastern half of 
the country. Chilly temperatures are expected with the chance for 
scattered light precipitation Thursday and Friday. As the upper 
trough moves away to the east over the weekend...dry and seasonable 
weather will return and continue into next week.

Through Tonight

Thin cirrus is slowing increasing across the region early this 
morning with patchy fog having developed in response to shallow 
moisture and largely calm flow in the near surface layer. 07Z 
temperatures ranged from the upper 30s to the mid 40s. 

Fog has remained localized to this point with visibilities largely 
remaining above one mile. The remnants of the weak boundary that 
moved into the forecast area on Tuesday appears to be located just 
south of Interstate 70 early this morning and may serve as a focal 
point for further expansion of the ongoing fog through the predawn 
hours as temperatures fall to the dewpoint. Will continue to monitor 
through daybreak with fog diminishing by mid morning.

The greater focus for today will be on the low pressure currently 
organizing over northwest Iowa early this morning. The low will 
continue to strengthen as it tracks southeast with an associated 
cold front today then across the forecast area late this afternoon 
and evening. Convection will rapidly develop along the boundary by 
late day and at least presents a sneaky yet conditional risk for a 
few severe storms. Initially the approach of the low and cold front 
will promote an increase in S/SW flow across the Ohio Valley with a 
narrow axis of subtly higher dewpoints and MLCAPE values from 600-
1200 j/kg drawn poleward along the front by mid afternoon. This will 
approach the Wabash Valley after 20Z with increasing convective 
development expected after that as BL shear increases and lapse 
rates steepen. Convection will surge east along the front with 
impacts from 21Z through about 01Z from northwest to southeast 
across the forecast area. 

The combination of best moisture and instability with strongest 
shear will occur just south of the surface low track with the 
greatest risk for a few severe storms focusing south of a line from 
near or just north of Terre Haute E/SE through Bloomington and 
Columbus. While the low level jet is not particularly impressive... 
it will not take much to pull some of the higher winds to the 
surface with any stronger cell in this zone across the southwest 
half of the forecast area. The presence of a narrow one to two hour 
timeframe with increasing 0-1km SRH and favorable directional shear 
through the boundary layer supports a low but non-zero threat for a 
tornado as well. Stronger cells will carry a risk for small hail but 
anticipated updraft strength is likely not to be sufficient for 
larger hail. The convective line will shift east quickly and be out 
of the forecast area by mid evening. 

Strong cold advection will commence immediately in the wake of the 
frontal passage with gusty N/NW winds developing. Scattered light 
showers will continue tonight focused largely across the northeast 
half of the forecast area as cyclonic flow aloft gradually 
establishes. Temperatures will fall quickly to around 40 by daybreak 
Thursday.

Thursday through Friday Night

The coldest air of the Fall so far arrives for Thursday and Friday as 
an upper trough amplifies and then closes off an upper low that will 
drop into the eastern Great Lakes by Friday night. Multiple waves 
will pivot around the flank of the upper level trough maintaining 
plenty of low level clouds and periodic precipitation through the 
period.

The strongest of the short waves will track across the region on 
Thursday. As it does so the wave will interact with strong cold 
advection and steepening mid level lapse rates to generate scattered 
to numerous light rain showers peaking in coverage during the 
afternoon and focused particularly across the northeast half of the 
forecast area. The addition of brisk northwest winds and broad 
stratus will make for a raw chilly day across the area with highs 
remaining in the 40s. 

Subtle ridging Thursday evening will aid in decreasing shower 
coverage but yet another shortwave will pivot across the region 
Friday morning which will maintain at least a broken stratus deck 
with the potential for renewed light precipitation that may linger 
into the day. A more pronounced northerly fetch off Lake Michigan 
Thursday night into early Friday supports the development of a more 
persistent north-south band of rain and snow across northwest 
Indiana
